content: The following are professional interpretations of the provided references: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines in 2021 on school health services, emphasizing the importance of integrating health promotion into educational settings to improve student well-being and academic outcomes. 2. WHO also released implementation guidance in 2021 for transforming schools into health-promoting environments, focusing on strategies to enhance physical, mental, and social health among students. 3. A 2019 press release by the United Nations Human Rights Council highlighted the urgent need to address housing rights for LGBT youth as part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) agenda. 4. The Office of the High Commissioner on Human Rights published a fact sheet in 2020 addressing homelessness among LGBTIQ+ youth, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions to protect this vulnerable population. 5. 6. A study by Carducci et al. (2021) identified gaps and priorities in assessing food environments for children and adolescents in lowand middle-income countries, highlighting the need for improved data and interventions. 7. UNICEF's 2019 report on school-to-work transitions explored strategies to support young people in successfully navigating the shift from education to employment. 8. WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs) emphasize principles such as human rights, gender equality, equity, inclusion, medical ethics, universal health coverage, and evidence-based public health approaches. 9. WHO's 2020 recommendations on population size estimates for men who have sex with men (MSM) provide critical data for planning and implementing HIV prevention and care programs. 10. Higgins et al. (2011) developed a tool for assessing the risk of bias in randomized trials, which has become a cornerstone of evidence-based research. 11. Sterne et al. (2016) introduced the ROBINS-I tool for evaluating bias in non-randomized studies of interventions, enhancing the rigor of observational research. 12. Desrosiers et al. (2019) conducted a pilot study in Washington, D.C. 13. DiClemente et al. (2014) evaluated an HIV/STI risk-reduction intervention for African American adolescent girls in juvenile detention centers, finding significant efficacy in reducing sexual risk behaviors. 14. L’Engle et al. (2014) tested a brief intervention to reduce alcohol use among female sex workers in Mombasa, Kenya, showing promising results in reducing risky behaviors. 15. Hao et al. (2012) compared enhanced versus standard voluntary counseling and testing for promoting condom use among MSM in China, demonstrating the benefits of tailored interventions. 16. El-Bassel et al. (2011) conducted a randomized trial in New York City to reduce dual risks of HIV and hepatitis C among low-income drug-using couples, highlighting the effectiveness of couple-based prevention strategies. 17. El-Bassel et al. (2014) evaluated a couple-based intervention in Kazakhstan to reduce risks for HIV, HCV, and STIs among drug-involved heterosexual couples, showing significant risk reductions. 18. El-Bassel et al. (2014) assessed the efficacy of a group-based multimedia HIV prevention intervention for drug-involved women under community supervision, demonstrating its potential to improve health outcomes. 19. Strathdee et al. (2013) reported reductions in HIV/STI incidence and injection equipment sharing among female sex workers who inject drugs, following a randomized controlled trial. 20. Eaton et al. (2018) tested a sexual risk-reduction intervention for STI prevention among MSM in the USA, finding it effective in reducing risky sexual behaviors. 21. Johnson et al. (2013) conducted a cost analysis of an HIV/STI/hepatitis prevention intervention for young men leaving prison, demonstrating its cost-effectiveness in improving health outcomes. 22. Burgos et al. (2016) evaluated the cost-effectiveness of combined sexual and injection risk-reduction interventions among female sex workers who inject drugs in Mexican border cities. 23. Stephenson et al. (2020) explored the feasibility of a telehealth intervention to increase HIV testing among transgender youth, showing promising results. 24. Moitra et al. (2020) conducted a pilot trial of a motivational interviewing-based PrEP intervention for MSM, demonstrating feasibility and acceptability. 25. The United Nations Independent Expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity published a 2020 report on conversion therapy, emphasizing its harmful effects and the need for global prohibition. 26. Velloza et al. (2021) reviewed interventions to improve daily medication adherence among adolescents and young adults, providing insights for enhancing youth PrEP services. 27. Schreck et al. (2021) reviewed the literature on slam practices, highlighting the need for harm reduction strategies among individuals engaging in high-risk drug use. 28. McCall et al. (2015) discussed the phenomenon of chemsex and its implications for public health, emphasizing the need for targeted interventions. 29. WHO's 2021 guidelines on digital health strategies outline recommendations for strengthening health systems through innovative technologies. 30. Cunningham et al. (2018) demonstrated the effectiveness of peer navigation interventions in sustaining viral suppression among HIV-positive individuals released from jail. 31. Reback et al. (2021) adapted peer health navigation and contingency management to improve HIV care outcomes among transgender women of color, showing significant advancements along the HIV care continuum. 32. Kerrigan et al. (2016) evaluated a multi-level intervention to improve HIV outcomes among female sex workers living with HIV in the Dominican Republic, demonstrating feasibility and effectiveness. 33. Micheni et al. (2017) explored health provider perspectives on improving antiretroviral therapy adherence among MSM in coastal Kenya, identifying key barriers and facilitators. 34. Pitpitan et al. (2020) assessed the acceptability of a community-based peer navigator model to engage key populations in HIV care in Tijuana, Mexico, highlighting its potential for improving care engagement. 35. WHO's 2016 guidelines for screening, care, and treatment of chronic hepatitis C infection provide comprehensive recommendations for managing this condition. 36. Grebely et al. (2014) examined factors influencing spontaneous clearance of acute hepatitis C virus infection, including sex, viral genotype, and genetic predispositions. 37. Hellard et al. (2016) emphasized the importance of local networks in achieving global hepatitis C elimination goals by 2030 through treatment and prevention strategies. 38. Falade-Nwulia et al. (2018) addressed the challenges of hepatitis C reinfection in the era of direct-acting antivirals, proposing strategies to mitigate this risk. 39. The European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) published updated recommendations in 2020 on the treatment of hepatitis C, incorporating the latest evidence on direct-acting antivirals. 40. Braun et al. (2021) conducted a treatment-as-prevention trial to eliminate hepatitis C among MSM living with HIV in Switzerland, demonstrating the feasibility of this approach. 41. Matthews et al. (2021) compared 6-week versus 12-week sofosbuvir/velpatasvir regimens for treating recently acquired hepatitis C, providing evidence for shorter treatment durations. 42. Liu et al. (2020) evaluated the economic impact of extending hepatitis C treatment to acute infections and early-stage fibrosis among people who inject drugs in developing countries, using China as a case study. 43. Mukherjee et al. (2021) modeled the cost-effectiveness of expanding immediate hepatitis C treatment among HIV-positive MSM in Bangkok, Thailand, to reduce incidence rates. 44. Popping et al. (2019) demonstrated the cost-effectiveness of early treatment for acute hepatitis C infection in HIV-infected MSM, emphasizing the benefits of timely intervention. 45. WHO's 2021 global strategy on digital health outlines a vision for leveraging technology to enhance health outcomes worldwide. 46. Young et al. (2013) conducted a cluster randomized trial to evaluate the use of social networking technologies as tools for HIV prevention, demonstrating their potential to reach at-risk populations. 47. Ross et al. (2016) assessed the impact of a social media campaign targeting MSM during a syphilis outbreak in Winnipeg, Canada, highlighting the role of digital outreach in STI prevention. 48. Zhu et al. (2019) evaluated the effects of a mobile health intervention to promote HIV self-testing among MSM in China, demonstrating its effectiveness in increasing testing rates. 49. Bauermeister et al. (2015) explored the acceptability and preliminary efficacy of an online HIV/STI testing intervention tailored for young MSM, showing promising results. 50. Fontenot et al. (2019) examined preferences for a mobile health tool designed to facilitate HPV vaccination among young MSM, providing insights for tool development. 51. Balán et al. (2019) developed the SMARTtest app to facilitate HIV and syphilis self-testing, result interpretation, and linkage to care, demonstrating its utility in improving sexual health outcomes. 52. Brennan et al. (2018) conducted qualitative interviews with service providers in Ontario, Canada, to explore the provision of online sexual health outreach for gay, bisexual, and queer men. 53. Fantus et al. (2017) identified ethical issues in online sexual health outreach for sexual and gender minorities, emphasizing the need for ethical guidelines in digital health interventions. 54. WHO's 2019 recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening provide a framework for integrating technology into healthcare delivery. 55. FHI 360's 2021 report outlines a vision for accelerating the impact of HIV programs through online interventions, emphasizing the role of digital tools in public health.
